title: Ageing, faults and the trend that finds them

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is one cell's impedance sit flat on its own baseline for ten quarters, then turn upward and climb past the threshold you pick, when you drag the quarters on.
interactive.title: The trend that finds the cell
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A vented lead-acid string of 24 cells stands in a row, each cell a small tile. Above it sits a chart of impedance in mΩ against quarters. It runs from quarter 0 at commissioning to quarter 24, six years on. A quarters scrubber runs from 0 to 24. Each quarter adds one impedance reading to every cell. The reading at quarter 0 is each cell's baseline. The data are an example. The healthy cells start anywhere from 0.46 to 0.54 mΩ. They stay flat, wobbling by up to 0.005 mΩ a quarter. Leaving cell 17 out, the other 23 cells average 0.50 mΩ with an SD of 0.02 mΩ. Cell 17 starts at 0.50 mΩ and stays flat for ten quarters. After quarter 10 it climbs 0.02 mΩ each quarter. So it reads 0.60 mΩ at quarter 15 and 0.78 mΩ at quarter 24. Tap a cell to plot its readings, with a dashed line at its own baseline. Three readouts follow the tapped cell. The rise from its own baseline is (reading − baseline) ÷ baseline × 100. The fitted slope is the least-squares line through its last 4 readings, in mΩ a quarter. Its SDs from the string's mean is (reading − mean of the other 23) ÷ their SD. A threshold picker draws one line at a time on the tapped cell's chart. '20% rise' draws a line 20% above its baseline, 0.60 mΩ for cell 17. '30 to 50% band' draws a band from 30% to 50% above it, 0.65 to 0.75 mΩ. '150% of nominal' draws a line at 150% of nominal, 0.75 mΩ. It takes the baseline as nominal. Cell 17 reaches them at quarters 15, 18 and 23. A capacity-test button discharges the string at the quarter shown. The example string is rated 200 Ah at the 10-hour rate, so it runs at 20 A. A clock runs until the string reaches its end voltage. Capacity is the hours run ÷ 10 × 100. That holds because ampere-hours are amps × hours at a fixed current. An 80% line is drawn at 8 hours. The hours are a sketch. They hold at 9.7 hours, 97%, up to quarter 10. Then they fall 0.38 hours each quarter, to 7.8 hours, 78%, at quarter 15. A charging-history picker opens the flagged cell as a cut-away. 'Float below the band' shows hard sulphate crystals on the negative plate. 'Long spells at low charge' shows dense acid sunk to the bottom, starving the tops of the plates. 'Float above the band' shows the positive grid thinning and shedding lead. 'Valve-regulated, charged hard' shows gas venting and the mat drying out. A tag on each says what can still be done. On a phone the three readouts and the picker's options wrap onto further lines, and no word splits. Each show screen has under about 90 words. Each ends on what its finished picture shows, so it reads well without the controls. Screen by screen. 0 asks a recall question. One cell's quarterly readings rise six times in a row. It asks whether that is drift or noise. First choice: drift, because a run of six one way is rare by chance. Second: noise, because readings always wobble. Third: neither, until a seventh reading is in. The right pick says 'Still there: a run of six one way points to a cause.' Hint for noise: noise goes up and down at random, so six rises in a row is unlikely. Hint for a seventh: six in a row is already the usual signal. 1 says to judge each cell against its own first reading, not against its neighbours. It shows the string of 24 cells. Each cell is read for impedance every quarter. Its first reading, at commissioning, is its baseline. Cells differ from new, here from 0.46 to 0.54 mΩ. So one reading on its own says little about a cell's health. Most resistance-based testers predict health little better than tossing a coin. Tap a cell to plot its readings against its own baseline. Once cell 17 climbs, another cell's say line adds that the band widens because cell 17 is climbing. It ends at quarter 8 with cell 17 plotted, flat on its 0.50 mΩ baseline. 2 says cell A was commissioned at 0.46 mΩ and now reads 0.53 mΩ. Cell B started at 0.54 mΩ and still reads 0.54 mΩ. The string averages 0.50 mΩ. It asks which cell to watch. First choice: A, because it has risen about 15% from its own baseline. Second: B, because it reads highest. Third: neither, because both sit near the string's average. The right pick says 'That's it: A has moved 0.07 mΩ from where it started. B has not moved.' Hint for B: B has read 0.54 mΩ since it was new. That is just how it was made. Hint for neither: the average hides a change. Each cell's own baseline shows it. 3 opens on its point: a steady climb one way is drift, not noise. It drags the quarters on. For ten quarters cell 17 stays flat, wobbling a little like the rest. Then it turns upward by 0.02 mΩ a quarter and keeps going. The fitted slope through its last four readings rises from about zero to 0.020 mΩ a quarter. Its rise from its own baseline reaches 20%. It sits 5 SDs from the string's mean. It ends at quarter 15, with cell 17 reading 0.60 mΩ. 4 says a cell's baseline was 0.50 mΩ and it now reads 0.60 mΩ. It asks how far it has risen from its baseline. The choices are 20%, 120% or 0.10%. The right pick says 'That's it: 0.10 ÷ 0.50 = 0.2, a 20% rise.' Hint for 120%: that is the new reading as a share of the baseline. The rise is only the extra. Hint for 0.10%: 0.10 is the rise in mΩ. Divide it by the baseline. 5 adds the threshold picker. How big a rise matters is argued. Published lines run from a 20% rise, through a 30 to 50% band, to 150% of nominal. So use your maker's or plant's. The 20% line sits at 0.60 mΩ. The band runs from 0.65 to 0.75 mΩ. The 150% line sits at 0.75 mΩ. Cell 17 reaches them at quarters 15, 18 and 23. Pick one to draw it. It ends with the 20% line drawn. 6 says a cell has risen 25% from its baseline, and its trend still climbs. It asks what to do. First choice: book a capacity test, because the rise only flags the cell. Second: replace it, because it is past 20%. Third: leave it, because it is under 30%. The right pick says 'That's it: the trend points, and the test decides.' Hint for replace: a rise in impedance says where to look, not how much capacity is gone. Hint for leave: another line already flags it. And the trend is still climbing. 7 runs the capacity test. The example string is rated 200 Ah at the 10-hour rate. So it is discharged at 20 A. The clock runs until the string reaches its end voltage. At a fixed current, ampere-hours are amps × hours. So capacity is the hours run ÷ 10 hours. The replacement line is 80%, at 8 hours. The weakest cell sets how long the string lasts, as in lesson 6. It ends at quarter 15, with the clock stopped at 7.8 hours, 78%, short of the line. 8 says a string rated for 10 hours at 20 A reaches its end voltage after 8.5 hours. It asks what the test says. First choice: 85% of rated capacity, above the 80% line, so keep it and keep trending. Second: 85%, so replace it, because it has lost 15%. Third: too close to call, so test it again. The right pick says 'That's it: 8.5 ÷ 10 = 85%, and the line is 80%.' Hint for replace: every battery loses some capacity with age. The line is 80%. Hint for test again: one clean full discharge is the answer. The trend says when to test next. 9 opens the flagged cell. The trend says which cell. The test says how much it has lost. The charging record says why. A history picker shows four faults. Keep a cell short of full charge, and soft sulphate hardens into crystals on the negative plate. Leave it at low charge with shallow cycles, and the acid sinks and starves the tops of the plates. Float it too high for too long, and the positive grid softens and sheds. Charge a valve-regulated cell too hard, and it vents its gas and dries out. It ends on sulphation. 10 says a flooded string's float was set below the maker's band for a year. It asks which fault to expect. First choice: sulphation on the negative plates. Second: corrosion of the positive grid. Third: dry-out. The right pick says 'That's it: below the band the cells never quite reach full charge. So sulphate hardens.' Hint for corrosion: that speeds up when too high a voltage is held too long. Hint for dry-out: that comes from charging a valve-regulated cell too hard. This string floated too low. 11 tags each fault with what can still be done. An equalising charge is a deliberate overcharge of the whole string. It reverses sulphation that is caught in time. Its gassing also mixes stratified acid. Grid corrosion is permanent. A valve-regulated cell cannot be topped up, so dry-out stays. So the earlier the trend finds a cell, the more can still be saved. It ends with all four tags showing. 12, 13 and 14 mix the ideas. 12 says every cell in a flooded string has risen about 25% from its own baseline, all together. Cell 9 sits 0.3 SD from the string's mean. It asks whether the string is healthy. First choice: no, the whole string has drifted, so test its capacity. Second: yes, no cell stands out. Third: yes, 25% is under the 30% line. The right pick says 'That's it: comparing with the string finds an odd cell. Only each cell's own baseline shows them all ageing.' Hint for stands out: when every cell moves together, the mean moves with them. Hint for 30%: the lines disagree. 25% is already past one of them. 13 says the other 23 cells average 0.50 mΩ with an SD of 0.02 mΩ, and one cell reads 0.56 mΩ. It asks how unusual that is. First choice: 3 SDs out, rare by chance, so check its own trend. Second: only 0.06 mΩ out, so it is normal. Third: 3 SDs out, so replace it. The right pick says 'That's it: 0.06 ÷ 0.02 = 3 SDs. Chance alone seldom gives that.' Hint for 0.06: the spread sets the scale. Here the spread is 0.02 mΩ. Hint for replace: it may have read high since new. Its own trend and a capacity test decide. 14 says a valve-regulated string was left on boost charge for weeks, and now one cell's impedance climbs. It asks which fault fits, and whether an equalise will help. First choice: dry-out, and an equalise would make it worse. Second: sulphation, and an equalise will clear it. Third: stratification, and an equalise will mix it. The right pick says 'That's it: too much charge drove gas out of a cell that cannot be topped up.' Hint for sulphation: that follows too little charge. This string had too much. Hint for stratification: that follows long spells at low charge. And an equalise is more overcharge for a sealed cell.
interactive.ignores: The readings are example data, drawn so the turn is easy to see. Real cells tend to creep upward a little with age. Readings also shift with temperature and with where the test leads sit. The 150% line takes each cell's baseline as its nominal value. A real nominal value comes from the maker. The capacity-test hours are a sketch that falls steadily once the climb starts. Real capacity does not follow impedance so neatly. That is why the test is needed. Each fault is drawn on its own, but a real cell often carries more than one. Time is sped up.

explain.text:
A cell that is wearing out often shows it slowly. Its impedance creeps up from where it started. Picture each fault taking plate or acid out of the work. The current then has fewer paths, so the cell's impedance rises. So don't watch how high a cell reads. Watch how far it has moved from its own first reading. Trend that, and flag the cell that turns upward. Then prove it with a test of its capacity. That habit is agreed. How big a rise should worry you is not.

Cells differ from new. In the example string, healthy cells start anywhere from 0.46 to 0.54 mΩ. So one reading tells you little. Most resistance-based testers predict health little better than tossing a coin. Take each cell's first reading at commissioning as its [[baseline]]. Read every cell the same way at each inspection. Plot each one against its own baseline. Two tools you already have do the rest. The fitted slope says how fast a cell is drifting. The z-score says how odd it is among its neighbours. That is its distance from the string's mean, in SDs. In the example, cell 17 sits flat for ten quarters. Then it climbs 0.02 mΩ a quarter. By quarter 15 it reads 0.60 mΩ. That is a rise of 0.10 ÷ 0.50, or 20%.

How big a rise matters is still argued. In flooded cells, a 20% rise generally goes with about 80% capacity.[^1] Another line treats 30 to 50% above baseline as cause for concern.[^2] By a third, most cells are below 80% capacity once impedance reaches 150% of nominal.[^3] So the line on your chart is the maker's or the plant's. Crossing it flags the cell. A [[capacity test]] decides. You discharge the battery at a set current and time it to its end voltage. Ampere-hours are amps × hours. So the hours run ÷ the rated hours gives the capacity as a share of its rating. Two IEEE standards recommend replacing it when the capacity falls below 80% of its rating.[^4] In the example, 7.8 hours of a rated 10 is 78%. That is below the line.

The trend says which cell. The test says how much it has lost. The charging record says why. A float voltage set too low or too high can be the cause. Keep a cell short of a full charge for long, and soft lead sulphate turns into hard crystals on the negative plates. Leave it at low charge with shallow cycles and no full charge, and the acid stratifies. Positive grids corrode slowly with age anyway. Float them too high for too long and they corrode faster. A corroding grid softens and sheds its lead. Charge a valve-regulated cell too hard and it vents its gas and loses water. That is called [[dry-out]]. Sulphation can be reversed if it is caught in time, but corrosion is permanent. The example's readings are made up for teaching. Real cells tend to creep upward a little. **Trend each cell against its own baseline. Treat a steady climb as a flag. Let a capacity test against the 80% line decide.**

analogy.text: You already trend insulation resistance on a motor. A reading of 200 MΩ passes most tests. But say that winding read 2,000 MΩ for years. Then the fall is the warning. You judge the machine against its own history. Then you run a fuller test before you condemn it. A cell works the same way. Its own baseline matters more than one reading set against its neighbours.
analogy.breaks: The direction is the opposite. Insulation resistance falls as a winding fails, but a cell's impedance rises. The meaning differs too. Insulation resistance is itself the property that fails. Impedance only hints at what matters in a battery, which is its capacity. Proving capacity takes a full discharge.

practice.text:
Use this when you look after a standby battery or read its records.

- Take a baseline when the battery is new. Record each cell's impedance and voltage, and for vented cells its specific gravity. Run a capacity test as part of its acceptance.
- Read every cell the same way each time. Use the same test points, the same state of charge and a similar temperature.
- Log each cell's readings by date. Plot each one against its own baseline.
- Look for a steady climb, not one high reading. Fit a line through the last few readings and note its slope.
- Compare each cell with the string as well. If a cell sits far from the mean, check its own trend.
- Use the maker's or the plant's threshold. Published lines run from a 20% rise to 150% of nominal.
- Book a capacity test when a cell crosses the line, or when its slope stays up.
- Two IEEE standards recommend replacing when tested capacity falls below 80% of rating.
- Read the charging record for the cause. Then the next cell need not age the same way.

**Rule of thumb:** one reading points nowhere. A trend points at the cell, and the capacity test decides.

**Worked example:** A vented cell's baseline was 0.40 mΩ. Over the last four quarters it read 0.42, 0.44, 0.46 and 0.48 mΩ. That is a climb of 0.02 mΩ a quarter. The rise is 0.08 ÷ 0.40, or 20%. The other cells sit flat. So book a capacity test now. The string is rated for 10 hours at its test current. It reaches its end voltage after 7.5 hours. That is 7.5 ÷ 10, or 75%. It is below the 80% line, so by that line it is due for replacement. The float record shows months above the maker's band. That points to faster grid corrosion.

**Common mistakes**
- Chasing the highest reading instead of the biggest rise.
- Treating an impedance threshold as a pass or fail. It only says where to test.
- Judging cells only against the string's mean. That misses cells ageing together.
- Equalising again and again to cure one cell. Each equalise overcharges the whole string. Prolonged overcharge feeds grid corrosion.
- Replacing a cell without asking why it aged.
